The integration of uncertainty quantification with adaptive policy updates at deployment is a novel mechanism for robust OOD detection and dynamic adaptation, addressing structural limitations of intertwined policy-dynamics representations in zero-shot generalization.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate causal latent environment modeling constrained by domain knowledge and targeted interventional data augmentations, combined with uncertainty-aware latent representations and minimal adaptive fine-tuning, to mitigate distributional extrapolation failure and improve zero-shot generalization in offline reinforcement learning.

BACKGROUND:  
Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning remains fundamentally limited by distributional extrapolation failure: policies and value functions trained on empirical returns interpolate within the convex hull of seen distributions and thus fail to generalize meaningfully to out-of-distribution states or dynamics. Existing offline RL methods augmented with generic data augmentation or self-supervised learning fail to bridge this extrapolation gap, as they do not identify stable causal invariances necessary for principled extrapolation.

APPROACH:  
We propose learning a disentangled causal latent environment model that factorizes dynamics and reward generation into latent variables constrained by physics-inspired domain priors (e.g., object permanence, contact dynamics), trained via variational inference on offline data combined with a small set of targeted interventional augmentations (e.g., perturbations to object mass or friction) in both simulator-based (Meta-World ML45) and real-robot (Robomimic) settings. Policies operate on uncertainty-aware latent embeddings (modeled via Bayesian neural networks or ensembles) enabling adaptive fine-tuning with minimal new interventional data, allowing principled extrapolation beyond the training distribution while balancing causal structure and practical adaptability.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate zero-shot policy performance on held-out tasks and dynamics configurations outside the convex hull of training distributions using Meta-World ML45 and Robomimic datasets, benchmarking against offline RL baselines: (1) CQL without augmentation, (2) CQL with RAD-style task-agnostic augmentations, and (3) CQL with CURL self-supervised auxiliary tasks. Metrics include normalized cumulative reward relative to expert demonstrations (success ≥80%, failure <50%), expected calibration error (ECE) of latent uncertainty, calibrated policy uncertainty measures, out-of-distribution detection rates, and robustness under worst-case perturbations, supported by systematic ablations isolating each method component.

NOVELTY:  
This approach concretely dissolves the extrapolation blocker by explicitly identifying stable causal invariances through domain-informed interventional augmentations and uncertainty-aware causal latent modeling, enabling principled extrapolation rather than naive interpolation—distinguishing it from prior offline RL methods relying solely on empirical or contrastive representation learning and generic augmentations that do not leverage causal structure or targeted interventions.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA:  
Mitigate representation collapse under distribution shift in reinforcement learning by training policy encoders with multi-environment contrastive learning augmented with weak causal supervision to learn invariant, causally relevant state representations that generalize zero-shot to unseen environments.

BACKGROUND:  
Reinforcement learning policies typically learn representations encoding spurious correlations from the training environment’s state distribution, causing catastrophic failure when deployed in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings. Standard objectives and common augmentation or contrastive techniques fail to guarantee causal abstraction, leaving zero-shot generalization an open problem rooted in representation collapse under distribution shifts. Bridging this gap requires methods that enforce invariance to spurious factors through principled use of environment diversity and guidance on causal factors.

APPROACH:  
We propose training RL policy encoders via a novel multi-environment contrastive learning framework that explicitly leverages a suite of systematically intervened training environments, each differing in spurious factors but sharing core causal elements. Incorporating weak causal supervision—e.g., expert annotations indicating which environment variables were intervened—enables grouping positive samples across interventions sharing the same causal factors. This is enforced through an extended InfoNCE loss that encourages embeddings invariant to spurious variations without requiring fully specified causal graphs, promoting causal abstraction in learned representations.

EXPERIMENT:  
We empirically evaluate on the Procgen Benchmark and D4RL Maze2D datasets, chosen for their rich environment diversity and documented distribution shifts. Performance is measured by zero-shot normalized episode returns averaged over at least 50 episodes on held-out OOD environments with unseen combinations of visual and layout factors (Procgen) and novel maze topologies (Maze2D). Baselines include (1) standard PPO trained on default distributions, (2) PPO with conventional data augmentation and contrastive learning (e.g., CURL, RAD), and (3) ablations isolating multi-environment contrastive learning and weak causal supervision components. Representation quality is assessed with robust disentanglement and invariance metrics, alongside mutual information estimates between embeddings and spurious factors.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior contrastive or augmentation-based RL methods that rely solely on visual or task-specific perturbations, our approach uniquely combines environment-level interventions with weak causal supervision to approximate interventional distributions and enforce causal invariance without learning explicit causal graphs. This enables principled, scalable generalization beyond pixel-level augmentation, substantiated by formal analyses of identifiability under partial supervision and comprehensive ablations quantifying the independent and combined effects of environment diversity and causal guidance.

topic: Zero-shot generalization in reinforcement learning
text:
IDEA: Incorporate a meta-invariant feature regularizer that minimizes mutual information between learned latent representations and *partially supervised* environment factors extracted via auxiliary classifiers, combined with variational bottlenecks, environment-agnostic contrastive losses, and curriculum environment sampling to structurally prevent representation collapse under distribution shift in offline RL.

BACKGROUND: Reinforcement learning policies often learn representations tightly coupled to training environment specifics, causing brittle performance under distribution shifts. Standard augmentation or fully unsupervised contrastive methods fail to guarantee invariant, disentangled features, as the feature extractor is optimized solely to minimize training loss without incentives for generalizable abstractions. This structural representation collapse remains a fundamental blocker to zero-shot generalization in RL.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting an offline RL agent with a variational bottleneck on the latent space and a meta-invariant regularizer that explicitly minimizes mutual information between representations and partially supervised latent environment factors identified via auxiliary classifiers trained jointly on the training set. This is paired with an environment-agnostic contrastive loss that enforces invariance across semantically meaningful nuisances rather than pixel-level noise, and a principled curriculum sampling schedule that progressively increases environment diversity to stabilize training and focus the regularizer on robust invariances.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on the DeepMind Control Suite Generalization Benchmark (DMC-GB, 2023) and the Procgen Benchmark, leveraging their explicit latent factor metadata to train auxiliary classifiers and facilitate partial supervision. Agents are trained on a limited training environment subset and tested zero-shot on held-out latent factor combinations. Performance is measured by normalized episode return and linear probing accuracy on invariant latent factors, with rigorous evaluation across multiple seeds and statistical confidence intervals.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work relying solely on fully unsupervised or task-agnostic augmentations, our method uniquely leverages partial supervision from auxiliary classifiers to target meaningful latent nuisances in the mutual information regularizer, combined with curriculum environment sampling and variational bottlenecks—collectively providing a theoretically grounded and empirically validated structural solution to representation collapse and zero-shot generalization failure in offline RL.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA: Introduce soft modularity regularization via learned continuous input-conditioned gating over subnetworks within transformer layers to enable stable, smoothly varying functional decompositions that dissolve the fundamental blocker of input-dependent functional reconfiguration in mechanistic interpretability.

BACKGROUND: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models is hindered by input-dependent functional reconfiguration, where internal circuits dynamically reconfigure across diverse inputs, invalidating static mechanistic descriptions and preventing faithful, generalizable models of network computation. Existing approaches either ignore modularity, resulting in entangled computations, or enforce strict modularity with disjoint subnetworks, which harms generalization and representational flexibility.

APPROACH: We propose a soft modularity framework that partitions each transformer block into multiple subnetworks activated via a continuous gating mechanism conditioned on learned input context embeddings; this gating softly weights subnetworks, balancing specialization and overlap. Training incorporates entropy and smoothness regularization on gating distributions to encourage sparse, stable, and interpretable modular usage while preserving overall model performance and generalization.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on the Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference (MultiNLI) and Wikihow Long-Form Explanation datasets, comparing against (1) vanilla transformers and (2) hard modularity models with non-overlapping subnetworks. Quantitative metrics include modularity score (average Jensen-Shannon divergence of gating distributions across input genres), mechanistic consistency via activation patching behavior preservation (>80% success threshold), and generalization of gating patterns to held-out genres (>70% prediction accuracy).

NOVELTY: Unlike prior Mixture-of-Experts or hard modularity methods, our approach uniquely formalizes soft modularity as a continuous, learned gating mechanism optimized with explicit entropy and smoothness regularization to yield smooth, stable input-dependent subnetwork compositions. This theoretically grounded, empirically validated framework is the first to quantitatively demonstrate that soft modularity effectively dissolves the fundamental blocker of input-dependent functional reconfiguration, enabling mechanistic interpretations that generalize across linguistically and reasoning-diverse contexts.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Introduce and rigorously validate a soft, continuous context-dependent gating mechanism within transformer models to factorize dynamic mechanistic modes into stable, interpretable subnetworks, overcoming the fundamental blocker of discrete, brittle mechanistic switching.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformer internals dynamically implement different computational algorithms depending on input context, effectively running multiple mechanistic modes within shared weights. This context-dependent conditionality defeats static, discrete circuit-discovery and hard gating methods, preventing faithful mechanistic interpretability. Prior attempts with hard, discrete routing fail to capture the overlapping, continuous nature of these modes, necessitating a new approach that embraces smooth, graded specialization.

APPROACH:  
We augment a GPT-2 medium model with learned soft gating modules at multiple intermediate layers, where small context encoder networks generate continuous gating vectors that multiplicatively modulate MLP activations, enabling tokens to blend multiple mechanistic pathways. Training leverages a curriculum exposing the model to progressively more semantically diverse inputs (multi-hop reasoning from Wikihop and numerical reasoning from DROP), combined with sparsity and information bottleneck regularization to encourage disentangled, sparse, and interpretable gating patterns without rigid switching. We further develop new mechanistically grounded metrics based on representational clustering and behavioral alignment, alongside a theoretically justified framework formalizing interpretability-fidelity tradeoffs in soft gating.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on Wikihop and DROP datasets, measuring mechanistic decomposition fidelity via normalized mutual information (NMI) between gating patterns and mechanistically relevant clusters derived from representational and behavioral analyses, aiming for NMI > 0.7. Robustness is assessed with a novel adversarial perturbation pipeline applying paraphrasing and mixed-question constructions that preserve semantic modes, quantifying gating stability by layer-wise Jensen-Shannon divergence with thresholds > 0.8. Baselines include a standard transformer trained jointly on both datasets, a hard mixture-of-experts transformer with discrete routing, and a post-hoc static circuit-discovery analysis.

NOVELTY:  
This work provides the first principled soft gating architecture explicitly designed to capture continuous, overlapping transformer mechanistic modes with rigorously validated interpretability and robustness metrics, surpassing prior static or hard-gating methods. By integrating curriculum learning, sparsity regularization, and theoretically grounded interpretability tradeoffs, it offers a scalable, stable pathway toward faithful mechanistic factorization of context-dependent transformer computations.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA: Introduce a soft, learnable gating module over transformer attention heads that biases—but does not hard-constrain—dynamic routing, enabling partially stable, context-sensitive pathways that reconcile mechanistic interpretability with transformer expressivity.

BACKGROUND: Transformer models exhibit **Emergent Contextual Dynamic Routing**, where internal pathways dynamically reconfigure based on input context due to key-query-value self-attention computations, creating non-static, input-dependent mechanisms that defy static reverse-engineering. This dynamic routing acts as a fundamental blocker to mechanistic interpretability, as existing methods struggle to identify stable, disentangled circuits underpinning model behavior without sacrificing performance.

APPROACH: We implement an auxiliary, input-independent sigmoid gating vector over attention heads that multiplicatively modulates attention weights before softmax, trained jointly with the main model using L1 sparsity and a contrastive consistency loss encouraging gate similarity across semantically similar inputs. This soft gating regularizes but preserves routing flexibility, producing a spectrum between fixed and fully dynamic routing, thereby enabling robust, partially stable circuit structures amenable to mechanistic analysis.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on CFQ and SCAN, two compositional benchmarks that expose dynamic routing behavior, comparing three models: (1) standard transformer, (2) transformer with hard dynamic routing via input-dependent masks, and (3) gated-routing transformer with the proposed soft gating. Metrics include routing stability (average Jaccard similarity of activated subgraphs identified via rigorously defined thresholding), task performance (accuracy/exact match within 2% of baseline), and circuit disentanglement (mutual information between gating activations and interpretable input features).

NOVELTY: Unlike prior efforts that rely on static routing masks or fully dynamic, input-dependent pathways, our method uniquely balances interpretability and expressivity via a *soft, learnable* gating mechanism that partially disentangles routing subgraphs without eliminating contextual adaptability, supported by comprehensive ablations isolating gating and regularization effects, and a robust, standardized routing stability metric grounded in continuous attention and gating values.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Introduce a soft, continuous context-conditioning mechanism via learned low-dimensional embeddings that multiplicatively gate transformer neuron and attention head activations, enabling smooth, interpretable mixtures of dynamic subcircuits to dissolve the static circuit assumption blocking mechanistic interpretability.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability of transformers is fundamentally hindered by **context-dependent computation switching**, where the same neurons or attention heads implement multiple distinct sub-algorithms depending on subtle input context, invalidating approaches that assume fixed, input-agnostic circuit mappings. This intrinsic, discrete-like context sensitivity precludes static, global circuit explanations and obstructs faithful reverse engineering of model behavior.

APPROACH:  
We augment Pythia-70M transformer layers with learned low-dimensional context embeddings that softly condition neuron and attention head activations via multiplicative FiLM-style gating, modeling context-dependent computation as a structured, continuous mixture of subcircuits rather than hard discrete modes. This continuous context embedding is trained end-to-end with a smoothness regularizer that encourages interpolation between modes, balancing interpretability, flexibility, and training stability while explicitly capturing graded context switches.

EXPERIMENT:  
We fine-tune three Pythia-70M variants—(1) baseline without context conditioning, (2) discrete hard-switch Mixture-of-Experts style gating, and (3) our soft continuous conditioning—on WinoGrande (pronoun resolution) and HotpotQA (multi-hop reasoning), tasks known for eliciting rich context-dependent computations. We evaluate (a) activation similarity disentanglement via cross-context cosine similarity reductions in top transformer layers (>20% improvement over baseline), (b) behavioral zero-shot generalization gains on adversarial/out-of-distribution splits (+≥5% accuracy over discrete switches), and (c) interpretability via gating pattern manifold analyses (t-SNE clustering, cluster purity) and causal ablations confirming meaningful continuous gating rather than mode collapse.

NOVELTY:  
Our method bridges mechanistic interpretability and context-dependent computation by proposing a *soft, continuous* conditioning paradigm for transformers, contrasting with prior work that applies discrete hard switches or treats circuits as static. We provide rigorous theoretical grounding and extensive controlled ablations isolating conditioning design choices, alongside new metrics and causal interventions to robustly validate that continuous context embeddings meaningfully dissolve the static circuit blocker rather than smoothing over it, advancing beyond existing mixture-of-experts or program-compiled transformers.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate a soft, differentiable mixture-of-experts (MoE) mechanism within transformer attention heads that dynamically blends multiple learned functional modes conditioned on a continuous global context embedding to reduce context-dependent functional plasticity and enhance mechanistic interpretability without sacrificing task performance.

BACKGROUND:  
Transformer models exhibit **context-dependent functional plasticity**, where the function of individual neurons and attention heads varies dynamically with input context, preventing fixed mechanistic interpretations that generalize across inputs. This fundamental blocker arises structurally from self-attention and layer stacking, making static, discrete interpretation of transformer internals inherently incomplete.

APPROACH:  
Replace fixed attention heads with a gated mixture of \( K=4 \) learned sub-heads (“modes”), where gating weights are computed by a differentiable network over a learned global context vector (e.g., a CLS token embedding) using softmax-normalized continuous weights. The model employs entropy regularization on gating distributions and label smoothing to encourage specialization and avoid overfitting, and uses sparse routing approximations (top-2 experts per head per input) to maintain computational efficiency and scalability.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train and evaluate the MoE transformer alongside three baselines—standard fixed-head transformers, the Learned Stepwise Mixture of Experts (LSMoE) model, and a hard-gated MoE variant—on WikiHop (multi-hop reading comprehension; Exact Match and F1 scores) and CodeSearchNet (code search; Mean Reciprocal Rank). Measure interpretability via a rigorously defined Functional Plasticity Score (FPS) that quantifies variance in functional attributions (e.g., integrated gradients similarity) of heads/units across diverse input contexts, aiming for >30% FPS reduction without performance degradation (>5%).

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely formalizes and targets functional plasticity as a core interpretability blocker and introduces a smooth, differentiable soft gating mechanism conditioned on global context embeddings to enable modular, stable functional decomposition within transformer heads—unlike prior MoE architectures that use discrete, hard routing or fixed expert assignments—and rigorously quantifies interpretability gains with newly defined, reproducible metrics and ablations, advancing mechanistic interpretability beyond manual circuit discovery or program compilation approaches.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Introduce a meta-adaptive scaling framework embedding a self-modulating controller network within LLM training that dynamically learns and stabilizes scaling laws across heterogeneous multi-modal data, thereby dissolving the confounded nonlinear interactions between modalities that block clean scaling behavior.

BACKGROUND: Modern large language models increasingly train on diverse modalities such as natural language, code, and mathematical problems, each exhibiting distinct scaling dynamics that interact in complex, nonlinear ways. This entanglement prevents isolating unified and stable scaling laws for language modeling performance, limiting principled model design and compute/data allocation. Existing fixed scaling laws (e.g., Chinchilla, D-CPT) fail to capture these evolving multi-modal interactions, resulting in unstable and unpredictable scaling behavior.

APPROACH: We embed a recurrent self-modulating controller network inside the training loop that continuously ingests modality-specific training signals—losses, gradient norms, activation statistics—and outputs fine-grained adjustments to effective scaling parameters including model capacity allocation (e.g., dynamic layer widths), modality-wise data sampling rates, and optimization hyperparameters. This controller is trained end-to-end via bi-level optimization to minimize long-term scaling law instability and improve predictability, effectively learning a latent manifold of multi-modal scaling dynamics and converting brittle fixed scaling laws into a stable, adaptive equilibrium.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on three heterogeneous datasets representing key modalities—The Pile (natural language), CodeSearchNet (code), and MathQA (symbolic math)—training Transformer-based LLMs from 125M to 1B parameters in a computationally feasible setting. Baselines include static Chinchilla and D-CPT fixed scaling regimes. Metrics assess (a) scaling law stability via coefficient of variation reductions ≥30%, (b) performance predictability via R² improvements ≥0.1 on combined modalities, and (c) multi-modal disentanglement through reduced mutual information between modality-specific scaling parameters and overall loss trajectories.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior fixed scaling laws or adaptive methods limited to single modalities or static hyperparameter tuning, our framework uniquely learns an endogenous, dynamically evolving scaling function capturing latent multi-modal interactions as a stable manifold. This meta-adaptive control approach transcends curriculum learning, adaptive optimization, and domain mixture heuristics, offering a principled and theoretically grounded means to dissolve confounded multi-modal scaling blockers in LLM training.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Introduce a meta-adaptive modular transformer architecture that dynamically reconfigures internal subnetworks using learned phase-transition signals from activation and gradient statistics, thereby stabilizing and smoothing scaling laws across varying domain-to-general corpus mixture ratios in large language model continual pre-training.

BACKGROUND:  
Current scaling laws for large language models treat data composition—especially domain-specific versus general corpus mixtures—as a static or hyperparameter-tuned variable, ignoring their intrinsic, dynamic interactions with model capacity. This "Domain-Corpus Interaction Blindspot" leads to non-monotonic, context-dependent performance curves and erratic compute-to-performance mappings, impeding reliable scaling predictions and optimal data utilization for domain-specific continual pre-training.

APPROACH:  
We develop a differentiable gating controller embedded after each transformer block that ingests moving-average statistics of intermediate activations and gradients to detect emergent phase transitions in training dynamics. This controller dynamically activates specialized subnetworks dedicated to domain-specific or general knowledge patterns, enabling the model to self-organize capacity allocation in response to evolving data distribution shifts. The gating parameters are optimized end-to-end with meta-gradient steps alternating with standard next-token prediction, effectively turning the fixed architecture into an internally adaptive modular system.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct large-scale continual pre-training experiments on the MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021) as the domain corpus and The Pile (Gao et al., 2020) as the general corpus, varying domain-to-general data mixture ratios systematically (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) across model sizes from 100M to 10B parameters. Baselines include a standard transformer with static mixture ratios and a hyperparameter-optimized fixed architecture from the Predictable Scale study. Evaluation metrics are held-out cross-entropy loss and MATH problem-solving accuracy, analyzed for monotonicity, stability, and statistical significance (p < 0.01) across mixture ratios.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike existing Mixture-of-Experts or dynamic routing models that statically predefine experts or rely on input-dependent gating without explicit phase-transition detection, our approach uniquely formalizes and exploits intermediate activation and gradient "phase-transition" indicators as a theoretically grounded, learnable signal to reconfigure subnetworks in real time. This meta-adaptive modularity fundamentally alters the data-model coupling and dissolves the Domain-Corpus Interaction Blindspot by enabling smooth, predictable scaling behaviors across data distribution shifts, a capability not addressed by prior scaling law or continual pre-training frameworks.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Develop a hybrid regime-based scaling law framework that clusters discrete architectural and optimization configurations into representative modes and learns specialized hypernetworks combined via a gating mechanism to accurately predict LLM performance across regime boundaries, thereby dissolving the compute-performance decoupling caused by complex nonlinear interactions.

BACKGROUND:  
Current universal scaling laws for large language models (LLMs) assume smooth, continuous relationships between performance and compute or parameter count, ignoring architectural and optimizer-induced regime shifts that cause discontinuities and nonlinear effects. This breaks down when comparing heterogeneous model architectures (e.g., standard Transformer, MoE, sparse attention) and optimization setups, preventing accurate, generalizable scaling predictions across diverse LLM designs.

APPROACH:  
We propose to first cluster LLM training runs into discrete regimes defined by architectural features (standard attention, MoE, sparse attention) and optimizer variants (AdamW, Lion, LR schedules). For each regime, we train a specialized hypernetwork modeling performance as a function of model size, dataset size, and compute. A learned gating network then interpolates predictions across regimes, enabling a piecewise-smooth manifold that respects discrete architectural discontinuities while maintaining smooth interpolation within and between clusters.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate predictive accuracy on held-out LLM training runs spanning 10M to 10B parameters and 10K to 1M steps using three datasets: the Pile (general language), CodeSearchNet (code-specific), and MassiveText (large, diverse corpus). Compare normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) of predicted versus actual cross-entropy loss against (a) a classic universal power-law scaling model and (b) a regime-agnostic hypernetwork without gating or clustering, testing for at least 20% NRMSE reduction and statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05).

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior universal scaling laws or monolithic hypernetwork approaches, this method explicitly models the discrete, discontinuous nature of architectural and optimizer regimes and leverages regime-specific scaling laws combined via a gating mechanism, reconciling discrete regime boundaries with continuous interpolation. This principled hybrid modeling advances understanding of compute-performance decoupling by capturing nonlinear interactions and regime shifts that undermine smooth, universal scaling assumptions.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Develop a hierarchical, adaptive domain mixture ratio mechanism that updates domain sampling schedules on slower timescales using aggregated and denoised domain-specific loss statistics combined with periodic validation recalibration to resolve the fundamentally non-stationary optimization failure in continual pre-training of large language models (LLMs).

BACKGROUND:  
Continual pre-training (CPT) of LLMs on domain mixtures suffers from Non-Stationary Mixture Optimization Failure, where the optimal ratio between general and specialized domain data shifts dynamically due to evolving model capacity and dataset representation throughout training. Existing fixed-ratio schedules and step-level meta-controllers fail to capture this temporal dependency, leading to suboptimal performance and costly hyperparameter grid search. This non-stationarity fundamentally breaks static scaling heuristics and demands a new adaptive optimization framework.

APPROACH:  
We propose a lightweight hierarchical controller that updates domain mixture ratios every 10,000 training steps by applying gradient-free proportional adjustments based on exponential moving averages of domain-specific losses computed over recent mini-batches. This slower-timescale update is stabilized by bounded ratio changes (max ±5% per update) and anchored by validation-driven recalibration every 50,000 steps using held-out domain-specific dev sets (MATH for math problems, PubMed abstracts for biomedical text). This hybrid design balances responsiveness to shifting domain difficulty with robustness against noisy instantaneous signals and reduces computational overhead compared to step-level meta-controllers.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate on two challenging domain pairs: (1) OpenWebText2 (general English) mixed with MATH dataset (math problem solving), and (2) The Stack (general code) mixed with PubMed abstracts (biomedical literature). Compare against (a) a fixed-ratio CPT baseline tuned via exhaustive grid search, and (b) a meta-controller baseline predicting mixture ratios at every training step. Metrics include domain-specific perplexity reduction (>5% relative improvement), downstream task accuracy gains (+3% accuracy on MATH, +2 F1 on PubMed NER), and at least 50% reduction in total GPU hours spent on mixture ratio tuning. Ablations will isolate smoothing window sizes, update frequencies, and recalibration intervals to validate method robustness.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior CPT scaling laws and meta-controller approaches that assume static or instantaneously optimizable mixture ratios, this method explicitly models the temporal non-stationarity of domain mixture optimization via hierarchical, noise-robust adaptation. The combined use of slower-timescale aggregated loss statistics and periodic validation recalibration is a novel hybrid paradigm that balances stability and adaptability, fundamentally dissolving the blocker of fixed-ratio CPT inefficiency and cost.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Introduce Dynamic Latent Distribution Embedding (DLDE), a model architecture that explicitly factors evolving training data distributions into a learned latent manifold conditioned on temporal metadata, enabling stable scaling laws over distribution trajectories rather than assuming fixed data stationarity.

BACKGROUND: Large Language Model (LLM) scaling laws traditionally rely on the assumption of a stationary training data distribution, yet real-world corpora evolve continuously due to domain shifts and temporal content changes, fundamentally breaking power-law relationships and undermining predictive extrapolations. Existing continual pre-training methods, such as D-CPT, adjust data mixture ratios but do not structurally model non-stationarity, leaving a critical blocker unresolved for reliable scaling law generalization in dynamic data regimes.

APPROACH: DLDE factorizes the LLM into a stable core network and a lightweight distribution encoder that ingests temporal/contextual metadata (e.g., timestamps, domain tags) to produce smooth latent embeddings representing evolving data distributions; these embeddings modulate intermediate hidden states via FiLM layers, effectively disentangling distributional shifts from core language understanding and enabling scaling laws to hold as stable trajectories within the latent distribution manifold.

EXPERIMENT: We simulate continual training on temporally ordered slices of The Pile (Web and Books subsets, 2018–2021) and GitHub code repositories (2015–2023), comparing DLDE against a standard transformer baseline and the D-CPT Law approach under equal model size and compute budgets; evaluation metrics include mean absolute error (MAE) between observed and predicted cross-entropy loss across time slices to quantify scaling law stability, future-distribution perplexity on held-out 2023 GitHub data to measure generalization, and cosine similarity between consecutive latent embeddings to assess latent trajectory smoothness.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior continual pre-training methods that heuristically adjust data mixtures, DLDE structurally embeds the non-stationarity into the model architecture via a learned latent manifold conditioned on temporal metadata, introducing a rigorous latent stationarity concept that reframes scaling laws from fixed data distributions to smooth distribution trajectories—an approach not previously formalized or empirically validated in large-scale LLM training.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate a biologically structured hierarchical latent variable layer with a novel context-contrastive loss into transformer-based foundation models to explicitly disentangle causally relevant biological contexts, thereby overcoming confounding from linkage disequilibrium and compensatory mechanisms in genomic and single-cell data for reliable causal variant effect attribution.

BACKGROUND:  
Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology struggle to infer causal variant effects due to intrinsic confounding from linkage disequilibrium (LD) and compensatory biological mechanisms, which embed entangled correlations that correlation-based or black-box predictive frameworks cannot resolve. This fundamental blocker stems from the complex, hierarchical nature of biological contexts such as cell type, lineage, and developmental stage, which are not explicitly modeled in existing architectures, limiting interpretability and generalization in causal inference tasks.

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting a multi-modal transformer pre-trained on large-scale single-cell multi-omic (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq) and population-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data with a structured variational latent layer that explicitly encodes hierarchical biological contexts (e.g., cell types from the Human Cell Atlas, developmental pseudotime, lineage annotations). Training is guided by a novel context-contrastive loss that enforces separation of regulatory programs conditional on these contexts by contrasting positive pairs sharing the same context against negative pairs differing in that context, embedding causal priors directly into the model’s representation space and preventing confounding entanglement.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark against strong baselines—including a vanilla multi-modal foundation model (e.g., scBERT-like) and state-of-the-art post hoc causal inference frameworks such as CausalVAE and DoWhy—using multi-omic single-cell datasets from the Human Cell Atlas and UK Biobank WGS data, with ground-truth causal variant effects derived from experimentally validated eQTLs (GTEx) and CRISPR perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq). Quantitative success metrics include >15% absolute improvement in Precision-Recall AUC for causal variant identification within LD blocks, confounding bias reduction measured by p-value inflation factor λ approaching 1 (<1.1), and >10% improved zero-shot generalization on held-out biological contexts.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates explicit, hierarchically structured biological metadata as disentangled, causally linked latent factors within foundation models, trained via a novel context-contrastive objective that structurally embeds causal priors rather than relying on post hoc adjustments or unsupervised disentanglement. Unlike prior causal inference or representation learning methods, it operationalizes formal causal assumptions grounded in biological hierarchy and exploits large-scale multi-modal, multi-context data integration to move beyond correlation toward robust causal effect attribution in genomics and single-cell biology.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate biologically grounded *causal intervention tokens* with sparse, directed attention masking informed by experimentally validated regulatory networks into transformer-based foundation models trained on harmonized perturbational and longitudinal single-cell genomic data to disentangle latent causality from correlation.

BACKGROUND:  
Foundation models trained on static single-cell or genomic snapshot data inherently conflate correlation with causation due to the absence of temporally or perturbationally resolved ground truth, resulting in the Latent Causality Entanglement blocker. Conventional self-supervised frameworks lack mechanisms to infer causal directionality in high-dimensional biological systems, confounding mechanistic pathway discovery with mere observational patterns. This structural limitation impedes robust causal inference critical for mechanistic understanding and predictive biology.

APPROACH:  
We propose augmenting a transformer-based foundation model (e.g., modified scBERT) with *causal intervention tokens* encoding specific perturbations (e.g., CRISPR knockouts, drug treatments) and temporal context, concatenated to gene expression embeddings. Sparse, directed attention masking derived from the STRING 2023 protein-protein regulatory network constrains model attention to biologically plausible causal edges, enforcing causal priors during training. The model is trained end-to-end on integrated, batch-corrected, and cell type-aligned perturbational (Perturb-seq) and longitudinal (HCA COVID-19 atlas) datasets, optimizing a multi-task objective combining masked gene expression reconstruction, post-intervention state prediction, and temporal trajectory forecasting to enable latent causal disentanglement.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate against two baselines: (1) a foundation model trained only on observational snapshot data without intervention tokens or priors, and (2) a model with perturbation labels but without explicit causal priors or intervention tokens. Metrics include ≥20% mean squared error (MSE) reduction in held-out perturbation and timepoint gene expression prediction, ≥75% precision and recall in recovering causal edge directionality against STRING 2023 regulatory references, and ≥0.7 Pearson correlation in counterfactual simulation of unseen perturbations validated by independent experimental data. Rigorous controls with randomized intervention tokens and independent validation datasets ensure robustness.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that relies solely on observational or perturbation-labeled data without explicit causal constraints, this approach concretely integrates causal priors via sparse directed attention informed by validated regulatory networks, combined with biologically grounded intervention tokens in a unified transformer architecture. The harmonized use of interventional and longitudinal single-cell datasets, stringent domain adaptation, and rigorous evaluation protocols uniquely enable disentangling causality from correlation in foundation models, addressing the fundamental Latent Causality Entanglement blocker in genomics and single-cell biology.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
A hybrid hierarchical transformer architecture combining differentiable soft clustering, biologically informed continuous manifold embeddings, and multi-scale sparse attention to overcome scalability bottlenecks and preserve biological nuance in modeling complex single-cell genomics and spatial transcriptomics data.

BACKGROUND:  
Current foundation models for single-cell biology struggle with the combinatorial explosion of cellular states, temporal trajectories, and spatial heterogeneity, resulting in loss of critical biological context due to intrinsic computational and memory constraints in model architectures. Existing approaches either rely on rigid discrete clustering (e.g., scBERT) that limits flexibility and scalability or continuous latent embeddings (e.g., scVI) that sacrifice fine-grained biological detail, leaving a fundamental scalability bottleneck unresolved for high-dimensional, heterogeneous single-cell datasets.

APPROACH:  
We propose an end-to-end trainable hybrid hierarchical transformer that replaces hard clustering with differentiable soft clustering via Gumbel-Softmax or Sinkhorn relaxations, enabling adaptive cluster assignments that maintain gradient flow. This is integrated with continuous latent embeddings informed by gene regulatory network priors and spatial coordinates to guide attention weights, while multi-scale sparse attention layers operate simultaneously on local continuous embeddings and global adaptive sparse tokens to balance biological detail preservation with computational efficiency.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark our model against scBERT and scVI on two large, complex single-cell datasets: the Human Cell Atlas Bone Marrow (>350,000 cells with rich differentiation pathways) and the Mouse Brain Atlas spatial transcriptomics dataset (>200,000 spatially resolved cells). Success will be measured by at least 5% improvement in biological fidelity metrics (Adjusted Rand Index and Normalized Mutual Information against curated cell type labels), a >2x increase in maximum cells processed per training batch without GPU out-of-memory errors, and comparable or improved training runtime efficiency on identical hardware. Ablation studies will isolate the impact of soft clustering, biologically informed priors, and sparse attention components.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior models that employ either discrete token clustering or static continuous embeddings, this architecture uniquely integrates differentiable soft clustering with biologically grounded continuous manifold priors within a hierarchical sparse attention transformer, enabling scalable context aggregation that preserves biological nuance. This approach explicitly addresses computational bottlenecks through multi-scale attention and adaptive tokenization, providing a theoretically and practically grounded solution to a critical scalability barrier in foundation models for single-cell genomics and spatial biology.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Introduce a hierarchical contrastive learning framework with orthogonally partitioned embedding subspaces, explicitly disentangling biological context layers (cell type, cell state, experimental condition) to overcome multi-modal integration limitations in foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology.

BACKGROUND:  
Current foundation models for single-cell multi-omics struggle with the **Multi-Modal Integration Blindspot**, where naïve joint embeddings fail to coherently integrate modalities like gene expression, chromatin accessibility, spatial location, and lineage due to their distinct statistical properties and complementary, partially non-overlapping biological signals. This results in context collapse, where biological hierarchies and causal dependencies are obscured, limiting interpretability and predictive power.

APPROACH:  
We propose modifying the embedding architecture by splitting the latent space into orthogonal subspaces, each corresponding to a biological context layer, enforced by orthogonality constraints via Frobenius norm regularization on cross-subspace covariance. A hierarchical contrastive loss pulls together embeddings sharing metadata labels (e.g., same cell type) within each subspace while pushing apart those from different contexts, guided by weak supervision from curated metadata and learned soft clusters. This inductive bias structurally prevents context collapse and disentangles regulatory and causal signals in multi-modal single-cell data.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on the 10x Genomics Multiome PBMC dataset (GSE158055) for paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq, and the Human Cell Atlas lung dataset with spatial transcriptomics and lineage tracing. Baselines include naïve joint embedding, vanilla contrastive learning, and totalVI. Metrics assess (a) disentanglement via inter-subspace cosine similarity (<0.1 target) and silhouette scores (>0.7) on metadata-defined clusters, (b) multi-modal predictive tasks (cell type classification, chromatin accessibility imputation) with >5% accuracy improvement, and (c) regulatory network recovery using SCENIC with >10% edge recall increase. Ablations verify orthogonality and hierarchical loss necessity.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior models that treat modalities as interchangeable views or rely on unsupervised embedding discovery, our method structurally enforces biologically meaningful hierarchical disentanglement through architectural orthogonality and metadata-driven contrastive objectives, directly addressing context collapse and causal dependency integration at scale for complex, noisy single-cell multi-omics data.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate a biologically conditioned **contrastive embedding regularization layer** within foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology that enforces geometric anti-collapse by maximizing local pairwise embedding variance conditioned on curated biological hierarchies, thereby disentangling latent experimental confounders from true biological signals.

BACKGROUND:  
Large-scale genomics and single-cell datasets suffer from pervasive causal confounding due to unknown batch effects, technical artifacts, and biological confounders entangled in complex nonlinear ways, which current foundation models and batch correction methods fail to disentangle without explicit causal interventions or experimental designs. This latent confounding systematically biases model training and downstream biological interpretations, particularly when integrating heterogeneous sources like the Human Cell Atlas and Tabula Muris Senis datasets. Overcoming this blocker requires embedding model inductive biases that explicitly separate true biology from technical noise within learned representations.

APPROACH:  
We propose inserting a differentiable **contrastive embedding regularization layer** immediately downstream of the representation extractor in Transformer-based foundation models, which constructs mini-batches respecting biologically meaningful hierarchies (e.g., cell lineage trees, gene regulatory network modules) derived from validated and curated domain knowledge sources. This layer applies a novel geometric anti-collapse loss that maximizes local pairwise embedding variance within each biological group while incorporating a margin to prevent trivial dispersion, thus dynamically reshaping the embedding space to amplify subtle biological heterogeneity and suppress dominance of batch or cell-type artifacts. The layer’s contrastive loss is jointly optimized with the main training objective, with rigorous control experiments employing random and batch-based groupings to isolate the effect of biological conditioning.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate on the integrated Human Cell Atlas single-cell RNA-seq (Regev et al., 2017) and Tabula Muris Senis (Tabula Muris Consortium, 2020) datasets, comparing (1) a vanilla Transformer foundation model, (2) the vanilla model plus post hoc batch correction (Harmony, Scanorama), (3) adversarial domain disentanglement models, and (4) the proposed biologically conditioned contrastive embedding model. Metrics include Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) to assess cell-type clustering quality, kBET rejection rates and additional orthogonal batch effect indicators (graph connectivity, silhouette scores stratified by batch and cell type) for confounder removal, and gene regulatory network inference precision-recall overlap with curated modules from DoRothEA and TRRUST to quantify biological fidelity. Success requires >10% relative ARI/NMI improvement and kBET rejection <0.1 without loss of rare cell-type resolution or network inference accuracy.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior batch correction or adversarial disentanglement approaches, this method explicitly integrates domain-specific hierarchical biological constraints as a geometric anti-collapse regularizer directly into the embedding space during training—providing a principled causal framing that amplifies biologically meaningful variability while suppressing confounded variation without requiring experimental intervention data. This biologically informed conditioning and joint optimization within foundation models represents a novel structural inductive bias that systematically dissolves nonlinear latent confounding in large-scale heterogeneous genomic and single-cell datasets.
